title: At the window in Ostia (Confessions 9)
hookLine: mother and son talk of heaven at a window, and days later she dies

lines: MOTHER AND SON AT THE WINDOW.
cards: A port town at the mouth of the Tiber. A house with a small garden, and two people leaning on a windowsill, looking down into it, tired from a long road and waiting for a ship home to Africa.
One is Augustine, newly baptized. The other is his mother, Monica, who prayed and wept for him for years. Nobody else is in the room.
Nothing is planned. They just start talking. And by Augustine's own account, somewhere in that unplanned conversation, the two of them, for a moment, touch the very thing they're talking about.

teach.b: First, the subject. In book nine of the Confessions, Augustine says they asked each other what the eternal life of the saints would be like, the life Paul says no eye has seen and no ear has heard. Not small talk.

Second, the climb. As they talk, their minds rise past everything made: past the earth, the sky and the stars, past their own minds, until for one heartbeat they touch the wisdom by which all things were made.
Then they sigh, and come back down to the noise of human words, which begin and end. He doesn't claim they stayed there. It was a moment, and they wanted it to last.
Third, what Monica says afterward. Son, nothing in this life delights me anymore. There was one thing I wanted to stay alive for: to see you a Catholic Christian before I died.
God has given me that and more.

teach.h: WHAT AM I STILL DOING HERE?
teach.b: What am I still doing here? Fourth, the ending. A few days later she falls ill with a fever.
She tells her sons not to worry about where her body is buried. Lay it anywhere, she says.
Only remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are. And she dies there, far from home. Augustine held back his tears at the funeral, and wept later, alone, before God.
So the window isn't only a mystical peak. It's two people who loved each other, saying what mattered while there was still time.

how: Catholics honor Saint Monica and Saint Augustine on neighboring feast days, and Monica's request to be remembered at the altar is often recalled when Mass is offered for those who have died.

games.q: you're Monica, far from home and ill. your sons worry you'll be buried in a strange land. what do you say?
o: take me home, whatever it costs.
lay my body anywhere; remember me at the altar.
games.why: she tells them not to worry about the place. her one request is to be remembered at the altar of the Lord, wherever they are.

practice: Bring to mind one person you love but rarely talk with about anything deep, a parent, a grandparent, a friend, and think of one thing you'd want them to know if this were your window: what gives you hope, or simply, I'm glad you're my mother.
Hold the person and the sentence together for a while. If you pray, remember them before God, the way Monica asked to be remembered.

wordCard.voice: Monica. Augustine's mother, who talked with her son about heaven at a window in Ostia, days before she died. Today's word.
